source_text: Nec mirum, quod haec de ineffabili natura dicuntur, cum in his etiam rebus, quas corporeis oculis cernimus et corporeo sensu diiudicamus, tale aliquid accidat. nam cum de fonte interrogati non possumus dicere, quod ipse sit fluuius, nec de fluuio interrogati possumus eum fontem uocare, rursus potionem, quae de fonte uel fluuio est, nec fluuium possumus appellare nec fontem, tamen in hac trinitate aquam nominamus et cum de singulis quaeritur, singillatim aquam respondemus. nam si quaero, utrum in fonte aqua sit, respondetur aqua; et si quaeram, utrum aqua sit in fluuio, nihil aliud respondetur, et in illa potione non poterit alia esse responsio; nec tamen eas tres aquas, sed unam dicimus. sane cauendum est, ne quisquam ineffabilem illius maiestatis substantiam sicut fontem istum uisibilem atque corporeum uel fluuium uel potionem cogitet. in his enim aqua illa, quae nunc in fonte est, exit in fluuium nec in se manet; et cum de fluuio uel de fonte in potionem transit, non ibi permanet, unde sumitur. itaque fieri potest, ut eadem aqua nunc ad fontis appellationem pertineat, nunc ad fluuii, nunc ad potionis, cum in illa trinitate dixerimus non posse fieri, ut pater ipse aliquando sit filius, aliquando spiritus sanctus. sicut in arbore radix non est nisi radix nec robur est aliud quam robur nec ramos nisi ramos possumus dicere; non enim quod dicitur radix, potest dici et robur et rami; nec lignum, quod pertinet ad radicem, potest aliquo transitu nunc in radice esse, nunc in robore, nunc in ramis, sed tantummodo in radice, cum illa regula nominis maneat, ut radix lignum sit et robur lignum et rami lignum, nec tamen tria ligna dicantur, sed unum. aut si haec habent aliquam dissimilitudinem, ut possint non absurde tria ligna nominari, ut etiam tria ligna dici possunt propter firmitatis diuersitatem, illud certe omnes concedunt, si ex uno fonte tria pocula inpleantur, posse dici tria pocula, tres autem aquas non posse dici, sed omnino unam aquam, quamquam de singulis poculis interrogatus in quolibet horum aquam esse respondeas, quamuis nullus hic transitus fiat, sicut de fonte in fluuium dicebamus. sed haec non propter illius diuinae naturae similitudinem, sed propter uisibilium etiam unitatem corporalia exempla data sunt, ut intellegeretur fieri posse, ut aliqua tria non tantum singillatim, sed etiam simul singulare nomen obtineant, ne quisquam miretur et absurdum putet, quod deum dicimus patrem, deum filium, deum spiritum sanctum nec tamen tres deos in ista trinitate, sed unum unamque substantiam.
thought_title: Visible unities as a hint of the Trinity's one substance
orientation: Augustine is explaining how three things can share one name and one substance, using visible examples to prepare for the claim that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.
pass_a_gloss: And it is not surprising that these things are said about the ineffable nature, since in those things also, which we discern with bodily eyes and judge with bodily sense, something of this kind happens. For when we are asked about a spring, we cannot say that it itself is the river, nor when asked about the river can we call it the spring; again, the drink, which is from the spring or the river, we can call neither the river nor the spring; yet in this trinity we name water, and when inquiry is made about the individual things, we answer water one by one. For if I ask whether there is water in the spring, the answer is water; and if I ask whether there is water in the river, nothing else is answered, and in that drink there cannot be another answer; yet we do not say three waters, but one. Certainly one must beware lest anyone think the ineffable substance of that majesty like this visible and bodily spring or river or drink. For in these things that water, which is now in the spring, goes out into the river and does not remain in itself; and when it passes from the river or from the spring into the drink, it does not remain there, from where it is taken. And so it can happen that the same water now belongs to the name of spring, now to the name of river, now to the name of drink, while in that Trinity we have said that it cannot happen that the Father himself is sometimes the Son, sometimes the Holy Spirit. As in a tree the root is nothing but root, nor can we call the trunk anything other than trunk, nor the branches anything but branches; for what is called root cannot be called both trunk and branches; nor can the wood, which belongs to the root, by some passage be now in the root, now in the trunk, now in the branches, but only in the root, while that rule of the name remains, that the root is wood and the trunk is wood and the branches are wood, and yet they are not called three woods, but one. Or if these things have some dissimilarity, so that they can not absurdly be named three woods, just as three woods can also be said because of the difference of firmness, that certainly all concede: if three cups are filled from one spring, three cups can be said, but three waters cannot be said, but entirely one water, although when asked about the individual cups you would answer that in any of them there is water, although no passage happens here, as we were saying about the spring into the river. But these bodily examples have been given not because of the likeness of that divine nature, but because of the unity even of visible things, so that it might be understood that it can happen that some three things obtain a singular name not only one by one, but also together, lest anyone be amazed and think it absurd that we say God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and yet not three gods in that Trinity, but one God and one substance.

choices.why: Glossary term for the one God in three persons; used here for the water example and the divine Trinity.
Glossary term for the underlying reality of God; Augustine uses it for the divine essence.
Robur means the hard wood of the tree, the trunk, as distinct from root and branches.
Poculum is a drinking vessel; 'cups' is the plain English equivalent.
Adverb meaning individually or separately; 'one by one' preserves the distributive sense.
Impersonal gerundive of obligation; preserves the warning force.

pass_b_english: And it is no wonder that such things are said about the ineffable nature, since something similar happens even with the things we see with bodily eyes and judge by bodily sense. For when we are asked about a spring, we cannot say that it is the river; and when we are asked about the river, we cannot call it the spring. Again, the drinking water that comes from the spring or the river we can call neither river nor spring. Yet in this trinity we name water, and when we are asked about each one separately, we answer 'water' for each. For if I ask whether there is water in the spring, the answer is water; and if I ask whether there is water in the river, nothing else is answered; and in that drinking water there can be no other answer. Yet we do not say there are three waters, but one.

Of course, one must beware lest anyone think of the ineffable substance of that majesty as being like this visible and bodily spring or river or drinking water. For in these, the water that is now in the spring flows out into the river and does not remain in itself; and when it passes from the river or the spring into the drinking water, it does not stay where it was taken from. So it can happen that the same water now belongs to the name of spring, now to the name of river, now to the name of drinking water. But in that Trinity we have said it cannot happen that the Father himself is sometimes the Son, sometimes the Holy Spirit.

In a tree, the root is nothing but root, and the trunk is nothing other than trunk, and we can call the branches nothing but branches. For what is called root cannot also be called trunk and branches; and the wood that belongs to the root cannot by some passage be now in the root, now in the trunk, now in the branches, but only in the root. Yet the rule of the name remains: the root is wood, the trunk is wood, the branches are wood, and still they are not called three woods, but one.

Or if these have some dissimilarity, so that they could without absurdity be named three woods—since they can indeed be called three woods because of the difference in their solidity—then certainly everyone grants this: if three cups are filled from one spring, they can be called three cups, but they cannot be called three waters. They are altogether one water, even though when asked about each cup individually you would answer that there is water in any one of them, although no passage takes place here as we said happens from the spring to the river.

But these bodily examples have been given not because of any likeness to that divine nature, but because of the unity that exists even among visible things. They are given so that it may be understood that it is possible for some three things to obtain a singular name not only one by one, but even all together. Then no one should be amazed or think it absurd that we call God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and yet not three gods in this Trinity, but one God and one substance.

problems.quote: they could not absurdly be named three woods
problems.source_quote: ut possint non absurde tria ligna nominari
problems.why: Latin says 'so that they COULD not absurdly be named' (possibility), English 'could not absurdly' misreads as 'could not be absurdly named' = impossible to name absurdly; should be 'could not absurdly be named' = 'could without absurdity be named'.
problems.fix: so that they could without absurdity be named three woods

edits.old: so that they could not absurdly be named three woods
edits.new: so that they could without absurdity be named three woods

fixed: Corrected 'could not absurdly be named' to 'could without absurdity be named' to match the Latin 'ut possint non absurde tria ligna nominari', which expresses possibility without absurdity, not impossibility of absurd naming.

last_rejected.quote: and does not remain in itself
last_rejected.source_quote: exit in fluuium nec in se manet
last_rejected.why: Latin says 'flows out into the river and does not remain in itself'; English omits 'flows out into the river'.
last_rejected.fix: flows out into the river and does not remain in itself
last_rejected.ruling: Prior clause 'flows out into the river' is present; 'nec in se manet' correctly rendered as 'does not remain in itself'.

last_rejected.quote: when it passes from the river or the spring into the drinking water
last_rejected.source_quote: cum de fluuio uel de fonte in potionem transit
last_rejected.why: Latin says 'from the river or from the spring'; English 'or the spring' loses the repeated 'de/from'.
last_rejected.fix: when it passes from the river or from the spring into the drinking water
last_rejected.ruling: 'from the river or the spring' correctly renders 'de fluuio uel de fonte'; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: it does not stay where it was taken from
last_rejected.why: Latin says 'it does not remain there, from where it is taken'; 'where it was taken from' slightly shifts meaning.
last_rejected.fix: it does not remain there, from where it is taken
last_rejected.ruling: 'where it was taken from' accurately renders 'ibi...unde sumitur'; no meaning changed.

last_rejected.quote: the wood that belongs to the root cannot by some passage be now in the root, now in the trunk, now in the branches
last_rejected.source_quote: nec lignum, quod pertinet ad radicem, potest aliquo transitu nunc in radice esse, nunc in robore, nunc in ramis
last_rejected.why: Again 'robur' rendered as 'trunk'; also 'lignum' is 'wood' not specifically 'the wood that belongs to the root'.
last_rejected.fix: nor can the wood that belongs to the root by any passage be now in the root, now in the hardwood, now in the branches
last_rejected.ruling: 'robur' as 'trunk' is standard; 'lignum quod pertinet ad radicem' = 'wood that belongs to the root'.

last_rejected.quote: since they can indeed be called three woods because of the difference in their solidity
last_rejected.source_quote: ut etiam tria ligna dici possunt propter firmitatis diuersitatem
last_rejected.why: Latin 'firmitatis' means 'firmness/strength/hardness'; 'solidity' is close but 'firmness' or 'hardness' better captures the quality of wood.
last_rejected.fix: since they can indeed be called three woods because of the difference in their firmness
last_rejected.ruling: 'solidity' is within normal range of 'firmitas'; mere preference for 'firmness'.

last_rejected.quote: although no passage takes place here as we said happens from the spring to the river
last_rejected.source_quote: quamuis nullus hic transitus fiat, sicut de fonte in fluuium dicebamus
last_rejected.why: Latin 'dicebamus' means 'we were saying'; English 'as we said' loses the imperfect sense of ongoing discussion.
last_rejected.fix: although no passage takes place here as we were saying happens from the spring to the river
last_rejected.ruling: 'as we said' adequately renders 'sicut...dicebamus'; imperfect tense nuance is not meaning-changing.

last_rejected.why: Latin says 'one and one substance' or 'one, one substance'; 'one God and one substance' adds 'God' not in the Latin, which says 'unum... substantiam'—the 'unum' refers back to 'deum'.
last_rejected.ruling: 'unum' refers to 'deum' (God); 'one God' correctly supplies the referent from context.
